claim: Activin A became very abundant during mouse and human bone fracture healing but was minimally detectable in intact bones.
source: Our data reveal that the transforming growth factor-β superfamily member Activin A became very abundant during mouse and human bone fracture healing but was minimally detectable in intact bones.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescent staining data in Figure 1 showing increased Activin A-positive cells after fracture, and qRT-PCR data showing nearly threefold increase in INHBA mRNA at fracture sites in human specimens.

claim: The Activin A-encoding gene Inhba was highly expressed in a unique, highly proliferative progenitor cell (PPC) population with a myofibroblast character that quickly emerged after fracture.
source: Single-cell RNA-sequencing revealed that the Activin A-encoding gene Inhba was highly expressed in a unique, highly proliferative progenitor cell (PPC) population with a myofibroblast character that quickly emerged after fracture
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data showing Inhba expression patterns in cluster 2 (PPCs), cell cycle analysis showing high proliferation in PPCs, and expression of myofibroblast markers in this population.

claim: PPCs represented the center of a developmental trajectory bifurcation producing cartilage and bone cells within callus.
source: Single-cell RNA-sequencing revealed that the Activin A-encoding gene Inhba was highly expressed in a unique, highly proliferative progenitor cell (PPC) population with a myofibroblast character that quickly emerged after fracture and represented the center of a developmental trajectory bifurcation producing cartilage and bone cells within callus.
evidence: Supported by Slingshot trajectory analysis and RNA velocity analysis showing PPCs at the center of developmental paths leading to chondrocytes and osteoblasts.

claim: Systemic administration of neutralizing Activin A antibody inhibited bone healing.
source: Systemic administration of neutralizing Activin A antibody inhibited bone healing.
evidence: Supported by histochemical analysis, μCT analysis, fracture healing scores, and mechanical testing showing reduced callus size, cartilage/bone areas, and mechanical properties in nActA.AB-treated mice compared to controls.

claim: A single recombinant Activin A implantation at fracture site in young and aged mice boosted PPC numbers.
source: In contrast, a single recombinant Activin A implantation at fracture site in young and aged mice boosted: PPC numbers
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry showing increased numbers of αSMA+ cells and pSMAD2+ cells within the αSMA+ population after Activin A treatment.

claim: A single recombinant Activin A implantation at fracture site in young and aged mice boosted phosphorylated SMAD2 signaling levels.
source: In contrast, a single recombinant Activin A implantation at fracture site in young and aged mice boosted: PPC numbers; phosphorylated SMAD2 signaling levels
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing increased percentage of pSMAD2+ cells in fracture calluses after Activin A implantation.

claim: A single recombinant Activin A implantation at fracture site in young and aged mice boosted bone repair and mechanical properties in endochondral and intramembranous healing models.
source: In contrast, a single recombinant Activin A implantation at fracture site in young and aged mice boosted: PPC numbers; phosphorylated SMAD2 signaling levels; and bone repair and mechanical properties in endochondral and intramembranous healing models.
evidence: Supported by histochemistry, μCT imaging, healing scores, and mechanical testing showing increased callus size, cartilage/bone areas, and improved mechanical properties in Activin A-treated mice. Also supported by drill-hole model data showing increased bone volume fraction.

claim: Activin A directly stimulated myofibroblastic differentiation in periosteal mesenchymal progenitor culture.
source: Activin A directly stimulated myofibroblastic differentiation, chondrogenesis and osteogenesis in periosteal mesenchymal progenitor culture.
evidence: Supported by in vitro data showing Activin A treatment up-regulated expression of myofibroblastic cell markers including αSMA/Acta2 and Tagln in periosteal cell cultures.

claim: Activin A directly stimulated chondrogenesis in periosteal mesenchymal progenitor culture.
source: Activin A directly stimulated myofibroblastic differentiation, chondrogenesis and osteogenesis in periosteal mesenchymal progenitor culture.
evidence: Supported by in vitro data showing Activin A treatment stimulated chondrogenesis as revealed by strong alcian blue staining and higher expression of cartilage markers Col2a1, Acan, and Sox9.

claim: Activin A directly stimulated osteogenesis in periosteal mesenchymal progenitor culture.
source: Activin A directly stimulated myofibroblastic differentiation, chondrogenesis and osteogenesis in periosteal mesenchymal progenitor culture.
evidence: Supported by in vitro data showing that neutralizing antibody treatment inhibited osteogenesis, indicating endogenous Activin A promotes osteogenic differentiation.

claim: Activin A was scanty in connective tissues of intact iliac periosteum but abundant at fracture site of long bones in human specimens.
source: Immunostaining of surgically retrieval bone specimens from patients showed that Activin A was scanty in connective tissues of intact iliac periosteum (Figure 1C, Intact) but abundant at fracture site of long bones (Figure 1C, Fracture).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry images in Figure 1C showing differential Activin A staining between intact and fractured human bone specimens.

claim: INHBA mRNA showed a nearly threefold increase at the fracture site in human specimens.
source: Real-Time Quantitative Reverse Transcription PCR Further analysis of these patient specimens showed a nearly threefold increase in INHBA mRNA at the fracture site (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D comparing INHBA expression in intact versus fractured human periosteal tissue samples.

claim: Activin A was detectable in only a few cells within the cambium layer of periosteum and in some bone marrow cells in intact control tibiae.
source: Immunofluorescent staining of intact control tibiae (Figure 1A, Intact) showed that Activin A was detectable in only a few cells within the cambium layer of periosteum (Figure 1Aa) and in some bone marrow cells (Figure 1Ab).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images in Figure 1A showing minimal Activin A staining in intact mouse tibiae.

claim: Five days after fracture, the number and distribution of Activin A-positive cells had dramatically increased.
source: Five days after fracture, the number and distribution of Activin A-positive cells had dramatically increased (Figure 1A, Fracture)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images in Figure 1A showing increased Activin A-positive cells at day 5 post-fracture.

claim: Activin A-positive cells five days after fracture included numerous fibroblastic-shaped cells within periosteum and round-shaped early chondrocytes within the developing soft callus.
source: Five days after fracture, the number and distribution of Activin A-positive cells had dramatically increased (Figure 1A, Fracture), and positive cells now included numerous fibroblastic-shaped cells within periosteum (Figure 1Ac) and round-shaped early chondrocytes within the developing soft callus (Figure 1Ad) co-staining with Sox9 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and immunohistochemistry images in Figure 1A and 1B showing Activin A-positive cells with different morphologies and co-staining with Sox9.

claim: Many Sox9+ chondrocytes within fracture callus produce Activin A.
source: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) of fracture sections indicates that many Sox9+ chondrocytes within fracture callus produce Activin A.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry images in Figure 1B showing co-localization of Activin A and Sox9 in chondrocytes.

claim: Marrow cells normally expressing the Activin A-encoding gene Inhba included mesenchymal progenitors and inflammatory cells such as granulocytes.
source: Marrow cells normally expressing the Activin A-encoding gene Inhba included mesenchymal progenitors and inflammatory cells such as granulocytes, based on our previous scRNA-seq analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Zhong et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by reference to previous scRNA-seq data and violin plot in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing Inhba expression in bone marrow cell populations.

claim: Bone fracture triggers local hematoma formation followed by an inflammatory cascade that involves innate and adaptive immune responses.
source: Given its traumatic nature, a bone fracture triggers local hematoma formation followed by an inflammatory cascade that involves innate and adaptive immune responses (Claes et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Claes et al., 2012, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Initial steps of fracture healing elicit the expansion and migration of the otherwise quiescent mesenchymal stem and progenitor cells within the periosteum.
source: These initial steps elicit the expansion and migration of the otherwise quiescent mesenchymal stem and progenitor cells within the periosteum that over time undergo differentiation into chondrocytes within the body of callus and osteoblasts at its peripheral ends.
evidence: Based on established understanding of fracture healing processes and supported by the scRNA-seq data showing expansion of progenitor populations after fracture.

claim: Mesenchymal stem and progenitor cells undergo differentiation into chondrocytes within the body of callus and osteoblasts at its peripheral ends over time.
source: These initial steps elicit the expansion and migration of the otherwise quiescent mesenchymal stem and progenitor cells within the periosteum that over time undergo differentiation into chondrocytes within the body of callus and osteoblasts at its peripheral ends.
evidence: Based on established understanding of fracture healing and supported by trajectory analysis showing differentiation paths from progenitors to chondrocytes and osteoblasts.

claim: Subsequent remodeling of callus routinely leads to nearly scar-less bone healing.
source: Subsequent remodeling of callus routinely leads to nearly scar-less bone healing.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about bone fracture healing outcomes.

claim: Fracture healing replicates and relies on many of the processes of endochondral and intramembranous ossification through which the skeleton normally develops and grows prenatally and postnatally.
source: Thus, fracture healing replicates, and relies on, many of the processes of endochondral and intramembranous ossification through which the skeleton normally develops and grows prenatally and postnatally (Lefebvre and Bhattaram, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lefebvre and Bhattaram, 2010, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: αSMA-expressing cells constitute about 4% of Cd45−Ter119−Cd31− cells in homeostatic mouse periosteum.
source: Using Acta2-CreER mice, the Kalajzic group recently demonstrated that αSMA+ cells constitute about 4% of Cd45−Ter119−Cd31− cells in homeostatic mouse periosteum and that DTA-mediated ablation of the cells severely reduces callus size after fracture (Matthews et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Matthews et al., 2021.

claim: DTA-mediated ablation of αSMA+ cells severely reduces callus size after fracture.
source: Using Acta2-CreER mice, the Kalajzic group recently demonstrated that αSMA+ cells constitute about 4% of Cd45−Ter119−Cd31− cells in homeostatic mouse periosteum and that DTA-mediated ablation of the cells severely reduces callus size after fracture (Matthews et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Matthews et al., 2021.

claim: A periosteum-resident Mx1+αSMA+ stem cell subpopulation expressed chemokine CCL receptors needed for effective bone healing.
source: Another report provided evidence of a periosteum-resident Mx1+αSMA+ stem cell subpopulation that expressed chemokine CCL receptors needed for effective bone healing (Ortinau et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ortinau et al., 2019.

claim: Insufficient bone fracture repair represents a major clinical and societal burden.
source: Insufficient bone fracture repair represents a major clinical and societal burden and novel strategies are needed to address it.
evidence: Based on established clinical knowledge about fracture healing complications.

claim: About 5–10% of patients experience healing deficiencies leading to problematic and costly non-unions.
source: These discoveries would also hold high clinical significance and importance as such knowledge could be leveraged to mitigate healing deficiencies seen in about 5–10% of patients, leading to problematic and costly non-unions that are not fully addressed by current therapeutic strategies (Hak et al., 2014; Tzioupis and Giannoudis, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hak et al., 2014 and Tzioupis and Giannoudis, 2007.

claim: Current therapeutic strategies do not fully address fracture non-unions.
source: These discoveries would also hold high clinical significance and importance as such knowledge could be leveraged to mitigate healing deficiencies seen in about 5–10% of patients, leading to problematic and costly non-unions that are not fully addressed by current therapeutic strategies (Hak et al., 2014; Tzioupis and Giannoudis, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hak et al., 2014 and Tzioupis and Giannoudis, 2007.

claim: Activin A has a role in promoting heterotopic ossification (HO) in mice.
source: Recent studies from our laboratories and others have revealed that the transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) superfamily member Activin A has a previously unsuspected role in promoting HO in mice (Hatsell et al., 2015; Hino et al., 2015; Mundy et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hatsell et al., 2015; Hino et al., 2015; Mundy et al., 2021.

claim: Activin A is produced by activated macrophages and regulates cytokine production and profile.
source: This protein is best known for its roles in inflammation where it is produced by activated macrophages and regulates cytokine production and profile (de Kretser et al., 2012; Morianos et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to de Kretser et al., 2012 and Morianos et al., 2019.

claim: Activin A has pro-chondrogenic activity on human and mouse progenitor cells.
source: The protein has also been found to have pro-chondrogenic activity on human and mouse progenitor cells (Mundy et al., 2021; Djouad et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mundy et al., 2021 and Djouad et al., 2010.

claim: Td+ cells in Col2a1-Cre;Gt(Rosa)26 tdTomato mice are major contributors to fracture callus.
source: Here, we selected Col2a1-Cre;Gt(Rosa)26 tdTomato (Col2/Td) reporter mice because as our previous study indicated, Td+ cells in these mice are major contributors to fracture callus (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2019 and by spatiotemporal analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In intact tibiae, the cortical bone surface was covered by a thin layer of periosteum mainly consisting of Td+ cells.
source: In intact tibiae, the cortical bone surface was covered by a thin layer of periosteum mainly consisting of Td+ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1Aa, Ba).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: At day 5 post fracture, Td+ cells had greatly expanded in number to form the thickened periosteum.
source: At day 5 post fracture, Td+ cells had greatly expanded in number to form the thickened periosteum (Figure 2—figure supplement 1Ab, Bb).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: By day 10, all chondrocytes as well as neighboring fibrotic cells were Td+.
source: By day 10 when cartilage reached its peak soft callus development as shown by Safranin O staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1Bc), all chondrocytes as well as neighboring fibrotic cells were Td+ (Figure 2—figure supplement 1Ac).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence and histological images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: By day 15, Td+ cells constituted the majority of osteoblasts and osteocytes in the callus.
source: By day 15 when most cartilage was undergoing endochondral ossification, Td+ cells now constituted the majority of osteoblasts and osteocytes in the callus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1Ad, Bd).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence and histological images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the remodeling bone present by day 30, the new periosteum at the edge of callus mostly consisted of Td+ cells.
source: In the remodeling bone present by day 30, the new periosteum at the edge of callus mostly consisted of Td+ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1Ae, Be).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence and histological images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Td+ cells, but not Td− cells, were able to form cell colonies in CFU-F assays of periosteal cells isolated from intact bones.
source: Colony-forming unit fibroblast (CFU-F) assays of periosteal cells isolated from intact bones revealed that Td+ cells, but not Td− cells, were able to form cell colonies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by CFU-F assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: The percentage of Td+ cells among freshly isolated periosteal cells increased from 2.8% at day 0 to 3.4% at day 5 and 8.5% at day 10.
source: The percentage of Td+ cells among freshly isolated cells increased from 2.8% at day 0 to 3.4% at day 5 and 8.5% at day 10 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: 7,496, 7,535, and 10,398 Td+ cells were sequenced from days 0, 5, and 10 samples, respectively, with a median of 3,462 genes/cell and 13,463 UMIs/cells.
source: Using the 10× Genomics approach, we sequenced 7,496, 7,535, and 10,398 Td+ cells from days 0, 5, and 10 samples, respectively, with a median of 3,462 genes/cell and 13,463 unique molecular identifiers (UMIs)/cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq quality control data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The merged scRNA-seq dataset comprising 25,429 cells resolved into 16 cell clusters.
source: We merged the resulting three datasets comprising an overall total of 25,429 cells that resolved into 16 cell clusters, including 6 clusters of periosteal mesenchymal lineage cells, 4 clusters of hematopoietic cells, 1 cluster of muscle cells, 1 cluster of synovial lining cells, 1 cluster of tendon cells, 1 cluster of endothelial cells (ECs), 1 cluster of Schwann cells, and 1 cluster of smooth muscle cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, D; Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by UMAP plots and cluster identification in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: Td expression was detected in all clusters but was highest in mesenchymal cells.
source: Td expression was detected in all clusters but was highest in mesenchymal cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by expression pattern shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: After removing non-mesenchymal cells, the recalculated data identified six distinct mesenchymal cell clusters.
source: Given the focus of our study on mesenchymal lineage cells in callus, we digitally removed those clusters as well as other non-mesenchymal cells. As a result, the recalculated data identified six distinct mesenchymal cell clusters (Figure 2A, B; Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by UMAP plots in Figure 2A and B showing six mesenchymal clusters.

claim: Clusters 3, 4, 5, and 6 represented early osteoblasts (EOB), osteoblasts (OB), chondrocytes (CH), and hypertrophic chondrocytes (HCH), respectively.
source: Based on lineage-specific traits, clusters 3, 4, 5, and 6 represented early osteoblasts (EOB), osteoblasts (OB), chondrocytes (CH), and hypertrophic chondrocytes (HCH), respectively (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by violin plots of cluster-specific markers in Figure 2C.

claim: Cells in cluster 1 were characterized by typical stem cell markers such as Cd34, Ly6a (Sca1), and Thy1 (Cd90), suggesting they represented mesenchymal progenitor cells (MPCs).
source: Cells in cluster 1 were characterized by several typical stem cell markers such as Cd34, Ly6a (Sca1), and Thy1 (Cd90), suggesting that they represented mesenchymal progenitor cells (MPCs).
evidence: Supported by violin plots in Figure 2C showing expression of stem cell markers in cluster 1.

claim: Cluster 2 cells markedly increased in number early from days 0 to 5.
source: When the merged datasets (Figure 2A) were separated by time point, it became clear that cluster 2 cells markedly increased in number early from days 0 to 5
evidence: Supported by UMAP plots separated by time point in Figure 2B and cell number estimates in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Chondrocytes (cluster 5), hypertrophic chondrocytes (cluster 6), and osteoblasts (clusters 3 and 4) expanded by day 10.
source: When the merged datasets (Figure 2A) were separated by time point, it became clear that cluster 2 cells markedly increased in number early from days 0 to 5, whereas chondrocytes (cluster 5), hypertrophic chondrocytes (cluster 6), and osteoblasts (clusters 3 and 4) expanded by day 10 (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by UMAP plots in Figure 2B and cell number estimates in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cluster 2 contained highly proliferative cells, particularly at day 5.
source: Interestingly, computational cell cycle analysis revealed that cluster 2 contained highly proliferative cells, particularly at day 5 (Figure 2D, E).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Several proliferation marker genes, such as Ccnd3, Cdk4, Cdc20, Cdca3, Mcm4, and Cepna, were highly expressed in cluster 2 at the day 5 time point.
source: Several proliferation marker genes, such as Ccnd3, Cdk4, Cdc20, Cdca3, Mcm4, and Cepna, were highly expressed in cluster 2 at the day 5 time point (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by violin plots of proliferation markers in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: RNA velocity analysis showed that directionality of cell differentiation and diversification started from cluster 1 (MPCs), advanced through cluster 2 (PPCs) and ended in cluster 4 (OBs) and cluster 6 (HCH).
source: Applying this approach to our merged datasets above (Figure 2A), we found that directionality of cell differentiation and diversification started from cluster 1 (MPCs), advanced and transitioned through cluster 2 (PPCs) and ended in cluster 4 (OBs) and cluster 6 (HCH) (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by RNA velocity analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Pseudotemporal cell trajectory analysis placed MPC cells at one end of the developmental trajectory, PPC cells in a central position, and OBs and CHs at the other two ends.
source: Likewise, at every time point, pseudotemporal cell trajectory analysis placed MPC cells (cluster 1) at one end of the developmental trajectory, PPC cells (cluster 2) in a central position, and OBs (cluster 4) and CHs (clusters 5 and 6) at the other two ends (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by Slingshot trajectory plots in Figure 2F.

claim: MPCs serve as stem/progenitors and give rise to PPCs which in turn diverge into chondrocytes and osteoblasts.
source: Together, the data strongly indicate that MPCs serve as stem/progenitors and give rise to PPCs which in turn diverge into chondrocytes and osteoblasts, contributing to soft and hard callus formation.
evidence: Based on integration of trajectory analysis, RNA velocity, and cell cycle data showing developmental relationships between cell clusters.

claim: The most up-regulated genes in PPCs indicated their myofibroblast-like phenotype.
source: In the merged dataset, the most up-regulated genes in PPCs indicated their myofibroblast-like phenotype.
evidence: Supported by GO term analysis in Figure 3A and expression of myofibroblast marker genes in Figure 3B.

claim: Up-regulated genes in PPCs were closely related to processes and pathways known to be regulated by myofibroblasts such as wound healing, focal adhesion, extracellular matrix organization, and contractile actin filament.
source: Those genes were closely related to processes and pathways known to be regulated by myofibroblasts such as wound healing, focal adhesion, extracellular matrix organization, and contractile actin filament (Hsia et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by GO term analysis in Figure 3A and citation to Hsia et al., 2016.

claim: Known myofibroblast marker genes such as Acta2, Tagln, Tagln2, Myl9, Actg1, Tpm2, and Fbn2 were up-regulated in PPCs.
source: Those genes were closely related to processes and pathways known to be regulated by myofibroblasts such as wound healing, focal adhesion, extracellular matrix organization, and contractile actin filament (Hsia et al., 2016), and included known myofibroblast marker genes such as Acta2, Tagln, Tagln2, Myl9, Actg1, Tpm2, and Fbn2 (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Hsia et al., 2016; López-Antona et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by violin plots in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and citations to Hsia et al., 2016 and López-Antona et al., 2022.

claim: The expression of myofibroblast marker genes was highly up-regulated at day 5 and then reduced at day 10.
source: The expression of these genes was highly up-regulated at day 5 and then reduced at day 10 (Figure 3B)
evidence: Supported by violin plots showing temporal expression patterns in Figure 3B.

claim: Fracture transiently promotes PPCs into a myofibroblast-like phenotype.
source: The expression of these genes was highly up-regulated at day 5 and then reduced at day 10 (Figure 3B), suggesting that fracture transiently promotes PPCs into a myofibroblast-like phenotype.
evidence: Based on temporal expression patterns of myofibroblast markers shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The least expressed genes in PPCs were those related to bone mineralization and chondrocyte differentiation.
source: Conversely, the least expressed genes were those related to bone mineralization and chondrocyte differentiation, confirming that the PPCs did not possess a terminally differentiated phenotype (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: Supported by GO term analysis in Figure 3A showing down-regulated pathways in PPCs.

claim: Compared to MPCs, PPCs highly expressed Inhba after fracture.
source: Particularly relevant to the present study was the finding that compared to MPCs, PPCs highly expressed Inhba after fracture (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by violin plots in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B showing Inhba expression patterns.

claim: Chondrocytes highly expressed Inhba, consistent with immunostaining results.
source: Note that chondrocytes also highly expressed Inhba, consistent with the immunostaining results shown in Figure 1.
evidence: Supported by violin plots in Figure 3C and immunostaining in Figure 1.

claim: The number of chondrocytes was much lower than PPCs in early callus.
source: However, their number was much lower than PPCs in early callus (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: Supported by cell number estimates in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: PPCs are likely to be the main source of Activin A in early fracture healing.
source: However, their number was much lower than PPCs in early callus (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), suggesting that PPCs are likely to be the main source of Activin A in early fracture healing.
evidence: Based on comparison of cell numbers and Inhba expression levels between PPCs and chondrocytes.

claim: Activin A binds to type II receptors (ActRIIA or ActRIIB) to recruit and phosphorylate type I receptors (ALK4 or ALK7) for initiating its intracellular signaling.
source: Activin A binds to type II receptors (ActRIIA or ActRIIB) to recruit and phosphorylate type I receptors (ALK4 or ALK7) for initiating its intracellular signaling (Pangas and Woodruff, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pangas and Woodruff, 2000, representing established knowledge about Activin A signaling.

claim: Genes encoding Activin A receptors (Acvr2a, Acvr2b, Acvr1b, and Acvr1c) were expressed in all mesenchymal progenitor populations.
source: uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) plots suggested that genes encoding these receptors (Acvr2a, Acvr2b, Acvr1b, and Acvr1c, respectively) were expressed in all mesenchymal progenitor populations
evidence: Supported by UMAP plots in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C showing receptor expression patterns.

claim: Acvr2a expression was enriched in MPCs.
source: uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) plots suggested that genes encoding these receptors (Acvr2a, Acvr2b, Acvr1b, and Acvr1c, respectively) were expressed in all mesenchymal progenitor populations and Acvr2a expression was enriched in MPCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by UMAP plots in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C showing Acvr2a expression pattern.

claim: MPCs were less proliferative than PPCs at both days 0 and 5.
source: EdU incorporation indicated that MPCs were less proliferative than PPCs at both days 0 and 5, though bone fracture did enhance proliferation in both populations (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation flow cytometry data in Figure 3D.

claim: Bone fracture enhanced proliferation in both MPCs and PPCs.
source: EdU incorporation indicated that MPCs were less proliferative than PPCs at both days 0 and 5, though bone fracture did enhance proliferation in both populations (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation flow cytometry data in Figure 3D comparing day 0 and day 5.

claim: Cd34+ cells highly expressed MPC markers including Cd34, Ly6a, Cd248, and Clec3b.
source: In addition, quantitative RT-PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis of cells sorted from day 5 callus verified that Cd34+ cells highly expressed MPC markers including Cd34, Ly6a, Cd248, and Clec3b
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3E showing expression of stem cell markers in sorted Cd34+ cells.

claim: Cd34− cells more strongly expressed myofibroblast markers (Acta2 and Tagln) as well as Inhba.
source: In addition, quantitative RT-PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis of cells sorted from day 5 callus verified that Cd34+ cells highly expressed MPC markers including Cd34, Ly6a, Cd248, and Clec3b, whereas Cd34− cells more strongly expressed myofibroblast markers (Acta2 and Tagln) as well as Inhba (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3E showing expression of myofibroblast markers and Inhba in sorted Cd34− cells.

claim: Many Td+ cells were positive for both αSMA and Activin A at day 5 post-fracture.
source: Lastly, immunohistochemistry (IHC) on day 5 fractures from Col2/Td mice revealed that many Td+ cells were positive for both αSMA and Activin A (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images in Figure 3F showing co-localization of αSMA and Activin A in Td+ cells.

claim: Double positive cells for αSMA and Activin A included not only progenitors but also early chondrocytes.
source: Those double positive cells included not only progenitors (Figure 3Fa) but also early chondrocytes (Figure 3Fb).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images in Figure 3F showing double positive cells in different locations.

claim: Activin A treatment stimulated cell proliferation in periosteal mesenchymal progenitor cultures.
source: Cell number analysis on day 3 indicated that Activin A treatment did stimulate cell proliferation, whereas treatment with nActA.AB inhibited it (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data in Figure 4A showing increased cell numbers with Activin A treatment.

claim: Treatment with nActA.AB inhibited cell proliferation in periosteal mesenchymal progenitor cultures.
source: Cell number analysis on day 3 indicated that Activin A treatment did stimulate cell proliferation, whereas treatment with nActA.AB inhibited it (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data in Figure 4A showing decreased cell numbers with nActA.AB treatment.

claim: Activin A treatment up-regulated the levels of expression of myofibroblastic cell markers including αSMA/Acta2 and Tagln.
source: Remarkably, Activin A treatment up-regulated the levels of expression of myofibroblastic cell markers including αSMA/Acta2 (Figure 4B, C) and Tagln (Figure 4C)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images in Figure 4B and qRT-PCR data in Figure 4C showing increased expression of myofibroblast markers.

claim: Treatment with recombinant TGF-β1 promoted myofibroblast development in periosteal cell cultures.
source: Remarkably, Activin A treatment up-regulated the levels of expression of myofibroblastic cell markers including αSMA/Acta2 (Figure 4B, C) and Tagln (Figure 4C) as did treatment with recombinant TGF-β1 which is known for its ability to promote myofibroblast development (Wynn, 2008).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images in Figure 4B and citation to Wynn, 2008.

claim: Activin A treatment stimulated chondrogenesis in periosteal cell cultures as revealed by strong alcian blue staining and higher expression of cartilage markers Col2a1, Acan, and Sox9.
source: The treatment did stimulate chondrogenesis versus control cultures as revealed by strong alcian blue staining and higher expression of such cartilage markers as Col2a1, Acan, and Sox9 (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: Supported by alcian blue staining in Figure 4D and qRT-PCR data in Figure 4E showing increased expression of chondrogenic markers.

claim: Activin A treatment did not appreciably enhance osteogenic differentiation in periosteal cell cultures.
source: Activin A treatment did not appreciably enhance osteogenic differentiation (Figure 4F, G).
evidence: Supported by alizarin red staining in Figure 4F and qRT-PCR data in Figure 4G showing no significant increase in osteogenic markers.

claim: nActA.AB treatment inhibited both osteogenesis and chondrogenesis in periosteal cell cultures.
source: However, nActA.AB treatment did inhibit both osteogenesis and chondrogenesis (Figure 4D–G).
evidence: Supported by alcian blue staining, alizarin red staining, and qRT-PCR data in Figure 4D-G showing decreased differentiation markers.

claim: Endogenous and exogenous Activin A acts to promote chondrogenic and osteogenic differentiation in periosteal progenitors.
source: Thus, endogenous and exogenous Activin A acts to promote chondrogenic and osteogenic differentiation in periosteal progenitors.
evidence: Based on in vitro differentiation assays showing effects of Activin A treatment and neutralizing antibody on chondrogenesis and osteogenesis.

claim: nActA.AB administration significantly reduced overall callus size and cartilage and bone areas at all time points post fracture (5, 7, 10, and 14 days) compared to isotype antibody controls.
source: Histochemical analysis clearly showed that nActA.AB administration significantly reduced overall callus size and cartilage and bone areas at all time points post fracture (5, 7, 10, and 14 days) compared to isotype antibody controls (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: Supported by Safranin O/Fast green staining images in Figure 5A and quantification in Figure 5B.

claim: Changes in callus volume and bone volume after nActA.AB treatment were verified by μCT analysis.
source: The changes in callus volume and bone volume were verified by micro-computed tomography (μCT) analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by μCT images and quantification in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: By 6 weeks, tibial fractures in the control group were all bridged, indicating successful recovery, but those in the nActA.AB treatment group were lagging, leading to a decrease in fracture healing score.
source: By 6 weeks in the control group, the tibial fractures were all bridged, indicating a successful recovery but those in the nActA.AB treatment group were lagging, leading to a decrease in fracture healing score (Figure 5C, p = 0.006).
evidence: Supported by fracture healing score data in Figure 5C showing statistically significant difference.

claim: Three-point bending analysis revealed 44.4%, 35.0%, and 29.0% reductions in energy to failure, stiffness, and peak load, respectively, in fractured tibias from nActA.AB- versus isotype-treated mice.
source: Furthermore, three-point bending analysis revealed 44.4%, 35.0%, and 29.0% reductions in energy to failure, stiffness, and peak load, respectively, in fractured tibias from nActA.AB- versus isotype-treated mice (Figure 5D), all statistically significant.
evidence: Supported by mechanical testing data in Figure 5D showing statistically significant reductions in mechanical properties.

claim: At day 7 post fracture, nActA.AB administration reduced the number of cells positive for phosphorylated SMAD2 (pSMAD2).
source: At day 7 post fracture, nActA.AB administration reduced the number of cells positive for phosphorylated SMAD2 (pSMAD2) through which Activin A normally signals intracellularly (Pangas and Woodruff, 2000), suggesting the effectiveness of neutralizing antibody treatment (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images and quantification in Figure 5E and F showing reduced pSMAD2+ cells.

claim: The number of PPCs positive for αSMA and the percentage of pSMAD2+ cells within PPC population were significantly decreased after nActA.AB administration.
source: Interestingly, the number of PPCs positive for αSMA and the percentage of pSMAD2+ cells within PPC population were significantly decreased, while the percentage of pSMAD2+ cells within non-PPCs remained the same.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification in Figure 5F showing differential effects on αSMA+ versus αSMA− populations.

claim: The percentage of pSMAD2+ cells within non-PPCs remained the same after nActA.AB administration.
source: Interestingly, the number of PPCs positive for αSMA and the percentage of pSMAD2+ cells within PPC population were significantly decreased, while the percentage of pSMAD2+ cells within non-PPCs remained the same.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification in Figure 5F showing no change in pSMAD2+ cells within αSMA− population.

claim: nActA.AB administration reduced gene expression of Acta2 and Inhba in fracture callus.
source: These data were further con firmed by reduced gene expression of Acta2 and Inhba in fracture callus after nActA.AB administration (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 5G showing reduced expression of Acta2 and Inhba.

claim: PPCs were the primary responsive cell type to Activin A in early fracture.
source: Taken together, our results clearly suggest that the PPCs were the primary responsive cell type to Activin A in early fracture
evidence: Based on differential response to nActA.AB treatment between αSMA+ and αSMA− populations shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Systemic interference of Activin A action by nActA.AB treatment impaired fracture healing.
source: Taken together, our results clearly suggest that the PPCs were the primary responsive cell type to Activin A in early fracture and that systemic interference of Activin A action by nActA.AB treatment impaired fracture healing.
evidence: Based on comprehensive data showing reduced callus formation, mechanical properties, and healing scores after nActA.AB treatment.

claim: Trabecular and cortical bone structure was essentially identical in nActA.AB- and control isotype-treated mice in contralateral, uninjured tibiae.
source: We also examined contralateral, uninjured tibiae in all mice above and asked whether Activin A normally regulates bone homeostasis. µCT scanning showed that trabecular and cortical bone structure was essentially identical in nActA.AB- and control isotype-treated mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by μCT analysis of uninjured femurs in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 showing no significant differences in bone parameters.

claim: Activin A does not have major homeostatic roles in bone, at least within the time frame of the studies.
source: µCT scanning showed that trabecular and cortical bone structure was essentially identical in nActA.AB- and control isotype-treated mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), indicating that Activin A does not have major homeostatic roles, at least within the time frame of our studies.
evidence: Based on μCT analysis showing no differences in bone structure in uninjured bones after nActA.AB treatment.

claim: Exogenous Activin A implantation increased callus size and cartilage and bone areas at each time point (5, 14, and 28 days) in both 2-month-old and 20-month-old mice.
source: Notably, exogenous Activin A implantation had clearly increased callus size and cartilage and bone areas at each time point and in both age groups, based on histochemistry (Figure 6A, B) and μCT imaging (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Safranin O/Fast green staining in Figure 6A, quantification in Figure 6B, and μCT images in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Activin A implantation elicited a major increase in the number of mesenchymal cells positive for pSMAD2 and αSMA in fracture calluses of young mice at day 5 post fracture.
source: IHC revealed that Activin A implantation had elicited a major increase in the number of mesenchymal cells positive for pSMAD2 and αSMA and the percentage of pSMAD2+ cells within αSMA+ population (but not within αSMA− population) in fracture calluses of young mice at day 5 post fracture (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images and quantification in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Activin A implantation increased the percentage of pSMAD2+ cells within αSMA+ population but not within αSMA− population.
source: IHC revealed that Activin A implantation had elicited a major increase in the number of mesenchymal cells positive for pSMAD2 and αSMA and the percentage of pSMAD2+ cells within αSMA+ population (but not within αSMA− population) in fracture calluses of young mice at day 5 post fracture (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 6D showing differential effects on αSMA+ versus αSMA− populations.

claim: Overall healing scores were significantly increased in both young and old mice at 6 weeks post fracture after Activin A implantation.
source: Importantly, overall healing scores were significantly increased in both young and old mice at 6 weeks post fracture (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by fracture healing score data in Figure 6E showing statistically significant increases.

claim: Mechanical testing revealed that energy to failure, stiffness, and peak load were all significantly increased by Activin A implantation in 20-month-old mice.
source: Mechanical testing revealed that energy to failure, stiffness, and peak load were all significantly increased by Activin A implantation in 20-month-old mice (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by mechanical testing data in Figure 6F showing statistically significant increases in mechanical properties for 20-month-old mice.

claim: Young mice had stronger bone than old mice with increased stiffness and peak load.
source: In line with previous reports (Liu et al., 2022), young mice had stronger bone than old mice with increased stiffness and peak load.
evidence: Supported by mechanical testing data in Figure 6F and citation to Liu et al., 2022.

claim: There was a trend of increase in energy to failure in young mice after Activin A treatment but it was not statistically significant.
source: We also noted a trend of increase in energy to failure in young mice as well after Activin A treatment but was not statistically significant.
evidence: Based on mechanical testing data in Figure 6F showing non-significant trend.

claim: Activin A implantation promotes a quick expansion of mesenchymal progenitors and a promotion of healing.
source: Taken together, the data indicate a quick expansion of mesenchymal progenitors and a promotion of healing following Activin A supplementation.
evidence: Based on comprehensive data showing increased progenitor markers, callus formation, and healing outcomes after Activin A treatment.

claim: In the drill-hole bone repair model, woven bone formation is usually observed by day 7 post-surgery, and bone bridging and re-corticalization occur by day 21.
source: In this model, woven bone formation is usually observed by day 7 post-surgery, and bone bridging and re-corticalization occur by day 21 (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2019 describing the drill-hole model characteristics.

claim: In control drill-hole samples, bone formation became evident in the medullary region of interest by day 7 post-surgery and extensive bone formation in the drilled region had occurred by day 21.
source: In all controls, bone formation became evident in the medullary region of interest by day 7 post-surgery and extensive bone formation in the drilled region had occurred by day 21 (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by μCT images in Figure 7A showing bone formation progression in control samples.

claim: Nearly all day 21 control drill-hole samples displayed complete defect bridging with bone volume fraction over 60%.
source: Nearly all day 21 samples displayed complete defect bridging and based on μCT-based sagittal and cross-sectional reconstitution, volume fraction of reconstituted bone (BV/TV) was over 60% (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by μCT quantification in Figure 7B showing BV/TV values.

claim: Systemic nActA.AB administration caused an appreciable reduction in bone deposition in both drilled and medullary regions by day 7 and a significant drop by day 21 compared to isotype controls in the drill-hole model.
source: Systemic nActA.AB administration caused an appreciable reduction in bone deposition in both drilled and medullary regions by day 7 and a significant drop by day 21 compared to isotype controls (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: Supported by μCT images in Figure 7A and quantification in Figure 7B showing reduced bone formation.

claim: Local supplementation of recombinant Activin A significantly increased BV/TV in medullary and drilled regions at both days 7 and 21 compared to vehicle controls in the drill-hole model.
source: Conversely, local supplementation of recombinant Activin A significantly increased BV/TV in medullary and drilled regions at both days 7 and 21 compared to vehicle controls (Figure 7C, D).
evidence: Supported by μCT images in Figure 7C and quantification in Figure 7D showing increased bone formation.

claim: Activin A promotes bone regeneration via intramembranous ossification.
source: Our data indicate that Activin A also promotes bone regeneration via intramembranous ossification.
evidence: Based on drill-hole model data showing effects of Activin A on intramembranous bone healing.

claim: Local implantation of recombinant Activin A stimulated fracture repair in rats.
source: Overall, our data and insights are very much in line with a previous study in rats in which local implantation of recombinant Activin A stimulated fracture repair (Sakai et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sakai et al., 1999.

claim: Endogenous Activin A is required for chondrogenic and osteogenic differentiation of human marrow mesenchymal stem cells.
source: They also agree quite well with siRNA studies showing that endogenous Activin A is required for chondrogenic and osteogenic differentiation of human marrow mesenchymal stem cells (Djouad et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Djouad et al., 2010.

claim: Activin A is an overall regulator and stimulator of the fracture repair process.
source: In sum, our study provides clear evidence that Activin A is an overall regulator and stimulator of the fracture repair process.
evidence: Based on comprehensive loss-of-function and gain-of-function studies showing effects on fracture healing.

claim: Activin A appears to act by promoting myofibroblastic, chondrogenic and osteogenic differentiation and ultimately bone healing.
source: The protein appears to act by promoting myofibroblastic, chondrogenic and osteogenic differentiation and ultimately bone healing, with the PPC population placed at the center of a developmental cascade aiding the progression of the overall process.
evidence: Based on in vitro differentiation assays and in vivo studies showing effects on multiple differentiation pathways.

claim: The PPC population is placed at the center of a developmental cascade aiding the progression of the fracture repair process.
source: The protein appears to act by promoting myofibroblastic, chondrogenic and osteogenic differentiation and ultimately bone healing, with the PPC population placed at the center of a developmental cascade aiding the progression of the overall process.
evidence: Based on trajectory analysis and functional studies showing PPCs as central to differentiation pathways.

claim: The distinct PPC population occupies an intermediate developmental step along the repair cascade.
source: The distinct PPC population identified here occupies an intermediate developmental step along the repair cascade and possesses a myofibroblast-like character after injury (Hinz, 2016).
evidence: Based on trajectory analysis showing PPCs between MPCs and differentiated cells, and expression of myofibroblast markers.

claim: Prior to fracture injury, the periosteum contains few PPCs.
source: Prior to fracture injury, the periosteum contains few PPCs, but fracture triggers a concerted response in which MPCs are rapidly activated to become PPCs, differentiating into chondrocytes and osteoblasts with time.
evidence: Based on scRNA-seq data showing low numbers of PPCs at day 0 and rapid expansion by day 5.

claim: Fracture triggers a concerted response in which MPCs are rapidly activated to become PPCs, differentiating into chondrocytes and osteoblasts with time.
source: Prior to fracture injury, the periosteum contains few PPCs, but fracture triggers a concerted response in which MPCs are rapidly activated to become PPCs, differentiating into chondrocytes and osteoblasts with time.
evidence: Based on trajectory analysis and temporal scRNA-seq data showing progression from MPCs to PPCs to differentiated cells.

claim: Based on cell prevalence, the PPCs appear to represent the bulk of cells within the thickening periosteum a few days after fracture.
source: Based on cell prevalence, the PPCs appear to represent the bulk of cells within the thickening periosteum a few days after fracture.
evidence: Based on cell number estimates in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B showing PPCs as the largest population at day 5.

claim: αSMA is often used as a marker of myofibroblasts in the tissue injury and regeneration field.
source: In the tissue injury and regeneration field, αSMA is often used as a marker of myofibroblasts, a cell population first discovered in skin wound healing studies and then identified as a key player in many tissue repair processes (Hinz, 2016; Pakshir et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hinz, 2016 and Pakshir et al., 2020, representing established knowledge.

claim: A recent scRNA-seq study identified an Lrrc15+ cell cluster that displays a αSMA+ myofibroblastic cell character and emerges only after injury in 13 injured and diseased mouse tissues including bone.
source: A recent scRNA-seq study isolated fibroblast cell populations from 13 injured and diseased mouse tissues including bone, and identified an Lrrc15+ cell cluster that displays a αSMA+ myofibroblastic cell character and emerges only after injury (Buechler et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buechler et al., 2021.

claim: Lrrc15 is a marker for PPCs in this study.
source: Interestingly, Lrrc15 is also a marker for PPCs in our study.
evidence: Based on scRNA-seq data showing Lrrc15 expression in PPCs.

claim: Abundant αSMA+ stromal cells were reported to occur around the injury site after metal implant surgery in mouse tibiae.
source: In addition, abundant αSMA+ stromal cells were recently reported to occur around the injury site after metal implant surgery in mouse tibiae (Vesprey et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vesprey et al., 2021.

claim: Acute injury resulting from bone fracture, metal implantation, or other insults appears to elicit a common and forceful repair response that is coupled to the emergence of progenitors with a myofibroblast-like phenotype.
source: In sum, acute injury resulting from bone fracture, metal implantation, or other insults appears to elicit a common and forceful repair response that is coupled to the emergence of progenitors with a myofibroblast-like phenotype.
evidence: Based on comparison of findings across multiple injury models and studies.

claim: Most of the previously identified progenitor cell markers including Cd200, Cd105 (Eng), and Cd51 (Itgav) are broadly expressed amongst periosteal mesenchymal populations.
source: Our data indicate also that most of the previously identified progenitor cell markers including Cd200, Cd105 (Eng), and Cd51 (Itgav) are broadly expressed amongst periosteal mesenchymal populations (Chan et al., 2015; Debnath et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by UMAP plots in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A and citations to Chan et al., 2015 and Debnath et al., 2018.

claim: MPCs appear to be quite similar to sorted Sca1+ and Cd90+ periosteal cells that have high CFU-F potential and multi-differentiation abilities.
source: These MPCs appear to be quite similar to those in a recent study indicating that sorted Sca1+ and Cd90+ periosteal cells have high CFU-F potential and multi-differentiation abilities (Matthews et al., 2021).
evidence: Based on comparison of marker expression and functional characteristics, supported by citation to Matthews et al., 2021.

claim: MPCs share a stem cell gene profile including Ly6a, Thy1, Cd34, and Clec3b that is similar to that of early mesenchymal progenitors previously identified in mouse bone marrow mesenchymal cells.
source: They also share a stem cell gene profile including Ly6a, Thy1, Cd34, and Clec3b that is similar to that of early mesenchymal progenitors previously identified in mouse bone marrow mesenchymal cells (Zhong et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on comparison of gene expression profiles and citation to Zhong et al., 2020.

claim: A global scRNA-seq study showed that fibroblasts in all tissues contain a most primitive cell cluster termed Pi16+ cells.
source: The recent global scRNA-seq study analyzing fibroblasts, defined as Pdgfrα+ cells, from 16 mouse tissues cited above showed that fibroblasts in all tissues, regardless of their states (steady and perturbed), contain a most primitive cell cluster termed Pi16+ cells (Buechler et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buechler et al., 2021.

claim: Markers of Pi16+ cells (Pi16, Dpp4, Ly6c1, and Dpt) are also MPC markers.
source: Notably, markers of Pi16+ cells (Pi16, Dpp4, Ly6c1, and Dpt) are also MPC markers (Figure 8—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by UMAP plots in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 showing expression of these markers in MPCs.

claim: MPC markers such as Ly6a and Cd34 are highly and specifically expressed in Pi16+ cells.
source: Notably, markers of Pi16+ cells (Pi16, Dpp4, Ly6c1, and Dpt) are also MPC markers (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), and MPC markers such as Ly6a and Cd34 are also highly and specifically expressed in Pi16+ cells (Buechler et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buechler et al., 2021.

claim: The data highlight the shared characteristics of fibroblast-like stem cells at different anatomic sites.
source: Together, the above data and insights highlight the shared characteristics of fibroblast-like stem cells at different anatomic sites.
evidence: Based on comparison of marker expression across different tissue types and studies.

claim: Inflammatory cells present at the fracture repair site include neutrophils and macrophages and release a spectrum of inflammatory and chemotactic mediators including members of the TNF and IL protein families.
source: Inflammatory cells present at the fracture repair site include neutrophils and macrophages and release a spectrum of inflammatory and chemotactic mediators including members of the TNF and IL protein families (Einhorn and Gerstenfeld, 2015; Loi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Einhorn and Gerstenfeld, 2015 and Loi et al., 2016, representing established knowledge.

claim: Inflammatory mediators are thought to lead to recruitment of fibroblasts, MSCs, and skeletogenic progenitors from local sources, propelling the next phase of skeletal tissue repair production and deposition.
source: These and other proteins are thought to lead to recruitment of fibroblasts, MSCs, and skeletogenic progenitors from local sources, propelling the next phase of skeletal tissue repair production and deposition (Gerstenfeld et al., 2001; Gerstenfeld et al., 2003), but details remain scant (Loi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gerstenfeld et al., 2001, Gerstenfeld et al., 2003, and Loi et al., 2016.

claim: Activin A may promote the initial inflammatory response needed for setting the repair process.
source: The previously described roles of Activin A in inflammation (de Kretser et al., 2012) suggest that the protein may promote the initial inflammatory response needed for setting the repair process.
evidence: Based on known roles of Activin A in inflammation and inference about its role in fracture healing.

claim: Activin A could represent a regulatory and functional nexus linking inflammation to local skeletogenic responses in diverse cell populations.
source: Together, previous studies and our current data lead to the important notion that Activin A could represent a regulatory and functional nexus linking inflammation to local skeletogenic responses in diverse cell populations and in turn, boosting fracture repair progression.
evidence: Based on integration of known inflammatory roles and demonstrated skeletogenic effects of Activin A.

claim: Activin A's capacity to play diverse biological roles could endow the protein with ideal characteristics as a therapeutic for fracture repair deficiencies.
source: Activin A's capacity to play such diverse biological roles could endow the protein with ideal characteristics as a therapeutic for fracture repair deficiencies.
evidence: Based on demonstrated effects on multiple cell types and stages of fracture healing.

claim: A variety of means have been tested in both animal studies and patients to improve fracture healing, but an effective and safe therapy is yet to emerge and be clinically applied.
source: A variety of means have been tested in both animal studies and patients to improve fracture healing, but an effective and safe therapy is yet to emerge and be clinically applied (Einhorn and Gerstenfeld, 2015; Roberts and Ke, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Einhorn and Gerstenfeld, 2015 and Roberts and Ke, 2018, representing current state of the field.

claim: Anabolic therapies utilize exogenous agents such as members of the BMP, FGF, Wnt, or hedgehog protein families and may not be as effective as desirable because of their targeting a given step or a given population mainly.
source: Anabolic therapies utilize exogenous agents such as members of the BMP, FGF, Wnt, or hedgehog protein families and may not be as effective as desirable because of their targeting a given step or a given population mainly (Roberts and Ke, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Roberts and Ke, 2018 and general knowledge about limitations of current therapies.

claim: Activin A may prove more effective than other anabolic therapies because of its early presence from the very onset of the fracture repair process and its activity through sequential populations.
source: Activin A may prove more effective because of its early presence from the very onset of the fracture repair process and its activity through sequential populations, including our newly described myofibroblast-like node toward terminal differentiation of cartilage and bone cells.
evidence: Based on demonstrated temporal expression patterns and effects on multiple cell types and differentiation pathways.

claim: The spectrum of biological and physiologic action by Activin A and the appreciable promotion of fracture repair provide a rational foundation and premise for the investigation of Activin A for clinical application.
source: Nonetheless, the spectrum of biological and physiologic action by Activin A and the appreciable promotion of fracture repair we demonstrate here provide a rational foundation and premise for the investigation of Activin A for clinical application.
evidence: Based on comprehensive functional studies showing therapeutic potential.
